PHASE 4 · ADVANCED PRIMARY CARE CLINICAL MANAGEMENT

Week 84 — Lesson 108: Gout & Hyperuricemia Management

FNP-level goal: Evaluate acute monoarthritis safely, distinguish gout from septic arthritis and other mimics, manage flare and long-term urate-lowering care within patient-specific safety limits, and support adherence, comorbidity management, and referral.

Learning Objectives

  • Recognize a typical gout flare while maintaining a differential that includes septic arthritis, crystal arthritis, trauma, and inflammatory disease.
  • Identify acute red-hot swollen joint/systemic illness features requiring urgent evaluation rather than empiric outpatient gout treatment.
  • Explain the difference between hyperuricemia, acute gout-flare treatment, and chronic urate-lowering therapy (ULT).
  • Apply treat-to-target urate follow-up and anti-inflammatory prophylaxis principles with CKD, drug-interaction, and hypersensitivity safety.
  • Assess tophi, kidney stones, cardiovascular/metabolic comorbidities, alcohol/diet patterns, access, and quality-of-life impact.

Part 1 — Hyperuricemia Is Not Synonymous With Gout

Gout is an inflammatory arthritis caused by deposition of monosodium urate crystals. It often causes abrupt severe pain, swelling, warmth, erythema, and tenderness in one joint, classically the first MTP joint, but any joint may be involved. Serum urate can support a longitudinal assessment, but an elevated level alone does not diagnose gout and a level measured during a flare may not reflect the patient’s usual baseline. Do not treat asymptomatic hyperuricemia as though it automatically requires the same plan as clinically active gout.

Ask about time course, prior similar episodes, joints involved, fever/systemic symptoms, trauma, wounds, surgery, immunosuppression, kidney disease, medications including diuretics, alcohol, diet, family history, tophi, nephrolithiasis, and functional effect. Examine joint(s), skin, temperature, range of motion, ability to bear weight, signs of infection, and evidence of tophi or chronic joint damage.

Part 2 — Acute Monoarthritis: Infection First

Gout and septic arthritis can coexist, and a classic-looking podagra does not eliminate infection. Acute severe monoarthritis with fever, systemic illness, marked pain on passive motion, bacteremia risk, immunosuppression, prosthetic joint, recent procedure, overlying cellulitis, inability to bear weight, or diagnostic uncertainty requires urgent in-person assessment. Arthrocentesis and synovial-fluid analysis may be needed to identify crystals and evaluate for infection. Do not reassure a patient with a hot swollen joint solely because they have a history of gout.

Part 3 — Treat the Flare and Treat the Disease Are Different Tasks

Acute flare therapy aims to control inflammation and pain; selection among anti-inflammatory options is individualized by symptom timing, kidney function, GI/cardiovascular risk, anticoagulation, diabetes, infection concern, medication interactions, pregnancy potential, and prior response. Repeated empiric steroid courses can worsen diabetes, hypertension, infection risk, mood, and bone health. Confirm the diagnosis and reassess patients with frequent flares rather than creating a cycle of refill-only care.

ULT reduces urate burden over time and is not simply an acute analgesic. It is strongly considered for patients with tophi, radiographic damage attributable to gout, or frequent flares, and may be considered in additional higher-risk contexts. Current ACR guidance favors a low starting dose with titration to a serum-urate target, typically below 6 mg/dL, rather than leaving patients on a fixed dose without follow-up. Starting or changing ULT can precipitate flares; anti-inflammatory prophylaxis and clear education are part of safe initiation.

Part 4 — Kidney Function, Hypersensitivity and Medication Safety

CKD is common in gout and changes both flare-treatment and ULT decisions, but it is not a reason to abandon long-term urate control. Allopurinol is a recommended first-line ULT option when indicated, including in CKD, with low-dose initiation and appropriate titration/monitoring. Patients of Southeast Asian ancestry (for example Han Chinese, Korean, or Thai) and African American patients may need HLA-B*58:01 testing before allopurinol according to current guidance because of higher prevalence and severe hypersensitivity risk. This decision must follow individualized history, ancestry, testing access, and prescribing guidance.

Reconcile diuretics, low-dose aspirin and other cardiovascular medicines, immunosuppressants, anticoagulants, OTC NSAIDs, supplements, and alcohol use. Do not stop an indicated cardiovascular medication merely because it may influence urate without weighing the full cardiovascular benefit/risk. Review rash, fever, mucosal symptoms, liver/kidney changes, severe GI effects, neuromuscular symptoms, and drug interactions promptly when therapy changes.

Part 5 — Lifestyle Care Without Blame

Dietary pattern, alcohol—especially beer and spirits—sugar-sweetened beverages, weight, hydration, and cardiometabolic health can influence flare risk, but gout is not a moral failure and is not caused by one meal. Use respectful, concrete counseling and coordinate hypertension, diabetes, obesity, CKD, sleep, and cardiovascular care. Ask what changes are affordable and sustainable; medication access, work schedules, cultural foods, and prior negative health-care experiences matter.

Part 6 — Monitoring, Referral and Recovery

Track flare frequency, joint function, work/sleep impact, serum urate when appropriate, kidney/liver function and other monitoring based on the regimen, tophi, stones, adherence, and adverse effects. Rheumatology referral is appropriate for uncertain diagnosis, recurrent flares despite goal-directed therapy, tophi, erosive disease, complex CKD/medication interactions, serious drug reaction, or possible alternative inflammatory disease. Reassess not only the number but whether the patient can walk, wear shoes, work, sleep, and participate in life.

Clinical Case

A 64-year-old with CKD, diabetes, and prior gout has a new hot swollen ankle with fever after a recent skin infection. The patient requests the usual prednisone refill.

FNP reasoning: previous gout does not make this automatically a gout flare. Fever, skin infection, and acute monoarthritis require urgent evaluation for septic arthritis before immunosuppression is continued or increased. After acute safety is addressed, review flare frequency, urate trend, kidney-safe long-term plan, and access barriers.

FNP Gout Framework

  1. Classify acute monoarthritis: gout pattern, infection/crystal/trauma alternatives, and immediate danger.
  2. Protect against missed infection: hot swollen joint plus systemic/host risk = urgent in-person pathway.
  3. Separate goals: acute flare control versus long-term urate reduction and crystal dissolution.
  4. Use treat-to-target follow-up: low-dose initiation/titration, serum-urate monitoring, prophylaxis, adherence, and side-effect review.
  5. Address whole-person risk: CKD, stones, cardiometabolic disease, lifestyle without stigma, function, access, and specialty care.

High-Yield Summary

Gout: is crystal-driven inflammatory arthritis; hyperuricemia alone does not equal gout.
Hot swollen joint: may be septic even with a gout history—do not miss infection.
Flare treatment: and chronic ULT have different purposes.
ULT: uses a treat-to-target strategy with monitoring and prophylaxis during initiation when appropriate.
CKD/safety: requires individualized selection, dosing, interaction and hypersensitivity review—not therapeutic nihilism.
FNP standard: protect against infection today and prevent painful, disabling future flares with feasible longitudinal care.

Clinical safety note: This lesson is educational. Acute monoarthritis evaluation, arthrocentesis, gout diagnosis, flare therapy, ULT selection/dosing/titration, HLA testing, monitoring, referral, and emergency disposition must follow current guidelines, local policy, collaboration/scope requirements, and the individual patient’s presentation.
